prize_parts.citation: For formalizing the political economy of trade policy, showing how lobbying and special-interest politics shape trade protection.

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged: a single-part prize on B001 for Grossman and Helpman, with a citation confined to the political economy of trade protection. The protection-for-sale framework turned a qualitative idea, that organised interests bend trade policy, into an equilibrium model with sharp cross-sector predictions. That is why it has been tested, qualified and extended for three decades. A framework that can be shown wrong in some settings is doing the work a scientific contribution should do. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: a long, tightly coupled partnership with joint papers and a joint book, so two names exclude nobody at the same level. Maturity is not in question. The round-1 exchange sharpened my case in one respect. Several members, supporters and non-supporters alike (Krusell, Enflo, Hassler), independently said the citation should not borrow from the growth-and-trade strand. I now treat the narrow wording as part of the case, not a drafting detail. Support counts are not merit, and I am not arguing from the number of first-place preferences. I weigh B001 on attribution clarity, durability of the framework and the discipline it imposed on later empirical work.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains empirical. Support for the protection-for-sale predictions is mixed and sensitive to specification and setting. A skeptic can say the prize would reward a research agenda rather than a settled result, and Krusell and Dreber both press this point. I come from design-based empirical work and should not undervalue theory, but I should equally not excuse a theory because it generated testing. The contribution is also narrower than the full Grossman-Helpman programme. Taken alone, the political-economy strand is less obviously prize-sized than a candidate with a large replicated empirical footprint. Helpman's separate credit on B030 means the committee must be explicit that it is rewarding one achievement. Statements in the files about the 2008 and 2025 prizes have not been independently verified. I cannot rule out that a better-informed colleague would find more overlap than I assume.

responses.point: Krusell prefers B002 (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) because three decades of use in merger review and antitrust validate BLP in practice. He now calls B001 a close alternative and says the cases differ in kind (method versus theory). He finds the mixed empirical record of protection-for-sale more worrying than I do, and he warns against widening the B001 citation to endogenous growth.
responses.response: We now agree on the citation. I would keep growth out of it, for the reason he gives. I accept that the empirical-record question is where we differ. His argument is that BLP is validated by use and B001 only by testing that partly fails. From a design-based perspective I would not equate use with confirmation. Random-coefficients estimation also depends on instrument validity and functional-form assumptions that I would want to see probed hard. B001's weakness is real, but it is a visible weakness in a framework built to be tested. Neither candidate is validated beyond doubt. The method-versus-discovery distinction does not decide it for me, since I rank B002 third and do not call a toolkit lesser. What keeps B001 ahead is attribution. Two names fit without an arbitrary cut, while B002 has to leave out Bresnahan and Reiss and separate Pakes's dynamic-games work from the demand framework. If the committee concluded that attribution in B002 can be settled with the BLP triple, I would regard it as a serious competitor and not merely a lower-ranked one.

responses.point: Dreber prefers B030 (Melitz and Helpman) because firm heterogeneity and selection have been confronted with micro data more densely than protection-for-sale. She treats mixed support for B001 as a reason to prefer B030. She names the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum omission as the main weakness and says the two Helpman ballots are not scientific competitors.
responses.response: I agree that the two ballots are different achievements and should be judged on how well established and how cleanly credited each is. I also take the empirical point seriously, since I raised the mixed record myself. My difficulty is that the density of testing she values partly concerns the exporter facts. As she acknowledges, Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum established those facts independently, and they are not credited. Much of the empirical support is therefore for a pattern the credited theory explains and did not discover. Testing that confirms a framework is stronger evidence for it than testing that fails. But when the facts have separate originators, a clean citation becomes harder. I said in round 1 that a committee might prefer to reward trade through the firm-heterogeneity line. Having read her case and the attribution discussion, I would not recommend that route as B030 is currently credited. If the committee found a defensible way to settle the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum question, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B018 for Autor, Dorn and Hanson. She moved from Katz to Dorn after the exchange and now words the citation around technology and trade shocks to labour demand, without claiming priority for the task framework. She treats the shift-share and persistence debates as evidence of maturity, and she acknowledges that B001 has cleaner attribution.
responses.response: Her revision answers my main round-1 objection. I said that replacing Dorn with Katz would mix two contributions, and the trio she now proposes follows the actual authorship of the China-shock papers. Narrowing the wording so it does not claim the task framework also removes most of my antecedent concern (Levy and Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo). I therefore move B018 up to my first alternative. We still differ on the identification debate. She sees open exchange between the authors and their critics on shift-share exposure designs and long-run persistence as maturity. I agree it is productive, but I would wait for it to settle before the prize rests on the magnitudes. Her point also lets me answer the chair's question. A trade-shock-only citation with a stable Autor-Dorn-Hanson set is a real prize candidate, and I would not oppose it in a later year. I still rank it behind B001 on attribution, because the B001 credit needs no such drafting and I regard the identification caveat as open.

responses.point: Teorell prefers B001 and would lead the citation with organised interests and trade policy, while naming the integration of innovation and growth into trade theory as supporting. He sees the 2008 and 2025 prizes as addressing different questions, but says he has not verified the 2025 details.
responses.response: We agree on laureates and on the lead strand. We differ on whether the growth strand should appear in the citation at all. Even in a supporting role, naming it puts it into the public claim and so asks the committee to defend the claim. Neither of us has verified how the 2025 prize relates to it, and I would not build a citation on a premise we cannot check. I accept his view that the growth-and-trade work is a different object from what the 2008 prize covered, and I do not treat that as a reason to exclude it from the background. The ballot's stated discovery is the political economy of trade policy, so the citation should say that. If the committee wants the broader programme recognised, it should decide that deliberately and show what the growth strand adds. It should not enter by implication.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the mixed empirical record of protection-for-sale to be a limit on the discovery or a normal feature of a framework that made its predictions testable. I cannot resolve this from the evidence in the files.
Whether the 2008 and 2025 prizes overlap with B001 enough to matter. I rely on colleagues' descriptions and have not checked them.
Whether a citation confined to trade-policy political economy is enough for a prize on its own. Colleagues who prefer the broader citation may see it as too narrow.
Whether the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum gap in B030 or the Dorn-Katz and task-antecedent questions in B018 could be settled so that either competes with B001 on attribution.

Whether the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises lowers appetite for B050 enough to change its place among my alternatives. No member prefers B050, and I cannot say what would make it a first choice.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the preferred configuration: neither Grossman nor Helpman appears among my listed co-authors or affiliations. For the alternatives, none of Autor, Dorn, Hanson, Katz, Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler or Gilchrist appears among my co-authors. My Uppsala-IFAU network (Holmlund, Edin, Åslund, Öckert, Johansson, Nybom) is not credited on any shortlisted ballot. Hjalmarsson lists Holmlund as a frequent co-author, and he is also a long-standing co-author of mine. That is a link between committee members, not a candidate-specific conflict. B018 and B017 are close to my own field of empirical labour economics, which I disclose as field proximity and not as a basis for recusal. I have tried to apply the same criteria to B018 as to B001. Conflicts are disclosed and not adjudicated.
